title: Binary Heap (Min / Max)
description: Min-heaps, max-heaps, 0-indexed array math, sift-up, sift-down, bottom-up O(n) build, and capacity limits on heap.html.

questions.prompt: In the 0-indexed array representation of a binary heap used by heap.html, where are the parent, left child, and right child of the node at index 4?
questions.explanation: With the root at index 0, heap.js uses parent(i) = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋, left(i) = 2i + 1, and right(i) = 2i + 2. For i = 4 that gives parent ⌊3 / 2⌋ = 1, left 2(4) + 1 = 9, and right 2(4) + 2 = 10. Answering parent 2, left 8, right 9 uses the 1-indexed formulas (⌊i / 2⌋, 2i, 2i + 1), which assume the root sits at index 1.
questions.page: On heap.html: build a heap of 11 values and inspect node [4] alongside its parent [1] and children [9] and [10].

questions.prompt: In a valid min-heap, the left child of a node must always be smaller than or equal to its right child.
questions.explanation: A min-heap only requires every parent to be ≤ each of its children; it places no ordering constraint between siblings. For example, [1, 10, 2] is a valid min-heap even though left child 10 is larger than right child 2. Requiring left < right confuses a binary heap with a Binary Search Tree (BST).
questions.page: On heap.html: select Min-Heap, enter 1, 10, 2 in Build Heap, and observe Heap Property stays Valid with 0 swaps.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of peeking at the minimum element of a min-heap (or the maximum element of a max-heap)?
questions.explanation: The root of the heap always sits at index 0 (A[0]), so peek() reads A[0] directly without modifying the tree or sifting any nodes, taking O(1) time. O(log n) is tempting because insert() and extract() sift along a root-to-leaf path, but peek() never sifts.
questions.page: On heap.html: press Peek Min (or Peek Max) and check the Binary Heap Complexity table.

questions.prompt: A min-heap currently has the array [5, 12, 8, 20, 15]. You insert 3. What is the heap array after sift-up finishes?
questions.hint: Append 3 at index 5, then compare with parent(5) = 2 and parent(2) = 0, swapping whenever 3 is smaller.
questions.explanation: 3 is placed at index 5 → [5, 12, 8, 20, 15, 3]. Its parent is index 2 (8): 3 < 8 so swap → [5, 12, 3, 20, 15, 8]. Its new parent is index 0 (5): 3 < 5 so swap → [3, 12, 5, 20, 15, 8]. Answering [3, 5, 8, 12, 15, 20] assumes inserting into a heap sorts the entire array, but sift-up only touches the single path from index 5 to the root.
questions.page: On heap.html: select Min-Heap, Build Heap with 5, 12, 8, 20, 15, then Insert 3 and step through sift-up.

questions.prompt: The array [40, 25, 30, 10, 20, 15] is a valid max-heap.
questions.explanation: Check every parent against its children: A[0] = 40 ≥ A[1] = 25 and A[2] = 30; A[1] = 25 ≥ A[3] = 10 and A[4] = 20; A[2] = 30 ≥ A[5] = 15. Every parent is ≥ its children, so it is a valid max-heap. Answering false usually happens because the array is not sorted in descending order (25 < 30 and 10 < 20), which a max-heap does not require.
questions.page: On heap.html: select Max-Heap, run Build Heap on 40, 25, 30, 10, 20, 15, and observe 0 swaps.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n values using bottom-up Floyd heapify (build)?
questions.explanation: Bottom-up build skips all leaves and sifts down internal nodes from parent(n − 1) down to 0. Half the nodes are leaves (0 work), a quarter sift down at most 1 level, an eighth at most 2, and the sum converges to O(n). O(n log n) is the tempting wrong answer because inserting n values one by one takes O(n log n), and multiplying n nodes by the full height log n gives a loose bound.
questions.page: On heap.html: read the "Why Build Heap Is O(n)" card and the Complexity table.

questions.prompt: A max-heap currently has the array [50, 30, 40, 10, 20, 15]. You call extract() to remove the maximum root. What is the heap array afterwards?
questions.hint: Move the last element (15) into index 0 to keep the tree complete, then sift it down toward the larger child.
questions.explanation: Extract removes 50 and moves the last leaf (15 at index 5) to index 0 → [15, 30, 40, 10, 20]. Comparing 15 with children 30 (index 1) and 40 (index 2), 40 is larger and beats 15, so swap index 0 and index 2 → [40, 30, 15, 10, 20]. Index 2 is now a leaf, so sift-down stops. Answering [40, 30, 20, 15, 10] assumes the heap is kept sorted, and shifting every element left would destroy the tree structure.
questions.page: On heap.html: select Max-Heap, Build Heap with 50, 30, 40, 10, 20, 15, then click Extract Max.

questions.prompt: When bottom-up build() heapifies an array of 10 elements (indices 0 through 9), which index does it sift down first?
questions.explanation: Bottom-up build starts at the last internal node, parent(n − 1) = parent(9) = ⌊(9 − 1) / 2⌋ = 4, because indices 5 through 9 have no children (2 × 5 + 1 = 11 ≥ 10) and are already valid 1-node heaps. Answering 5 uses ⌊n / 2⌋ instead of ⌊(n − 2) / 2⌋ and starts on a leaf; answering 0 starts top-down at the root instead of bottom-up.
questions.page: On heap.html: build a heap of 10 values and read Step 1 and Step 2 of Build Heap.

questions.prompt: Which of these binary heap operations have a worst-case time complexity of O(log n)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Insert and Extract each walk at most one root-to-leaf path in a complete binary tree of height ⌊log₂ n⌋, so both are O(log n) worst-case. Peek root reads A[0] in O(1), and bottom-up Build heap runs in O(n) total time, not O(log n).
questions.page: On heap.html: compare all rows in the Binary Heap Complexity & Properties table.

questions.prompt: In this visualizer's min-heap, inserting a value that equals its parent swaps the two equal nodes so the newly inserted value moves higher.
questions.explanation: heap.js uses strict comparison (a < b for min-heap, a > b for max-heap) so equal values never swap. When a child equals its parent, siftUp sees that the child is not strictly better and stops immediately with 0 swaps. Swapping equal values would waste work without changing the heap.
questions.page: On heap.html: Clear the Min-Heap, Insert 10, then Insert 10 again and check the swap count (0).

questions.prompt: Bottom-up build() creates a min-heap from [20, 15, 10, 30, 5, 8]. What is the resulting heap array?
questions.hint: Sift down index 2, then index 1, then index 0 (remembering to keep sifting 20 all the way down after it swaps with 5).
questions.explanation: lastParent = parent(5) = 2. Sift down i = 2 (10, child 8): swap → [20, 15, 8, 30, 5, 10]. Sift down i = 1 (15, children 30 and 5): swap with 5 → [20, 5, 8, 30, 15, 10]. Sift down i = 0 (20, children 5 and 8): swap with 5 → [5, 20, 8, 30, 15, 10], then continue at i = 1 (20, children 30 and 15): swap with 15 → [5, 15, 8, 30, 20, 10]. Answering [5, 10, 8, 30, 20, 15] is the result of inserting the six values one by one rather than running bottom-up build().
questions.page: On heap.html: select Min-Heap, enter 20, 15, 10, 30, 5, 8 in Build Heap, and step to the end.

questions.prompt: A min-heap has the array [2, 5, 5, 9, 10, 12]. You call extract() to remove the root 2. Because the two children of the root are tied at 5, which index does the moved value 12 end up at after sift-down finishes?
questions.hint: Move 12 to index 0. In heap.js, the left child wins ties during siftDown—and keep sifting until 12 settles.
questions.explanation: Removing 2 moves the last element 12 into index 0 → [12, 5, 5, 9, 10]. Its children at indices 1 and 2 are tied at 5; heap.js picks the left child (index 1) on a tie, swapping to [5, 12, 5, 9, 10]. Now 12 at index 1 has children 9 (index 3) and 10 (index 4), so it swaps with 9 to reach [5, 9, 5, 12, 10]—index 3. Answering 2 assumes the right child won the tie (where 12 would stop as a leaf at index 2); answering 1 forgets to continue sifting down.
questions.page: On heap.html: select Min-Heap, Build Heap with 2, 5, 5, 9, 10, 12, then click Extract Min.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for an arbitrary value x in a min-heap of n elements?
questions.explanation: A min-heap only guarantees parent ≤ child, not that smaller values lie in one subtree and larger values in the other. An arbitrary target x could sit at any leaf (roughly n / 2 nodes), so in the worst case you must inspect all n elements in O(n) time. O(log n) is tempting if you confuse a binary heap with a balanced Binary Search Tree (BST).

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about this visualizer's Binary Heap are true? Select all that apply.
choices: heap.html caps the interactive heap at 31 nodes (5 levels), while BinaryHeap.MAX_CAPACITY in heap.js is 63
extract() on an empty heap fails with a heap underflow error instead of returning -1
When two children tie during siftDown, the left child is chosen
The maximum value in a min-heap is always stored at the last index A[n - 1]
answer: heap.html caps the interactive heap at 31 nodes (5 levels), while BinaryHeap.MAX_CAPACITY in heap.js is 63
extract() on an empty heap fails with a heap underflow error instead of returning -1
When two children tie during siftDown, the left child is chosen
questions.explanation: heap-page.js sets HEAP_CAPACITY = 31 for readability while BinaryHeap.MAX_CAPACITY is 63; extract() on an empty heap returns a failure result (heap underflow) rather than a sentinel −1; and siftDown keeps best = left when both children are equal. The fourth statement is false because the maximum in a min-heap can appear at ANY leaf—for example, in [1, 10, 2] the maximum 10 is at index 1, not index 2.
questions.page: On heap.html: check Capacity 31 in the controls, Clear and press Extract Min to trigger underflow, and test [1, 10, 2].
